questions.q:
The stopping potential Vo (in volt) as a function of frequency (v) for a sodium emitter, is shown in the figure. The work function of sodium, form the data plotted in the figure, will be:
(Given: Planck’s constant h=6.63×10-34 J s , electron charge ( e ) =1.6×10-19 C)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
From Einstein's photoelectric equation, hν=ϕ+eV0  .

⇒V0=hνe-ϕe  ......1

At ν=4×1014 Hz, V0=0.

Putting the value in equation 1, we get

 0=hve-ϕe

So, Work function (ϕ)=hνe  in eV
=6.63×10-34×4×10141.6×10-19
=1.66 eV

questions.solution:
Expression for maximum kinetic energy can be written as, KEmax=E-ϕ

KEmax, 1=E1-ϕ=3.8-0.6=3.2 eV, KEmax, 2=E2-ϕ=1.4-0.6=0.8 eV

KEmax, 1KEmax, 2=3.20.8=4⇒4=12 mv1212 mv22 

⇒v12v22=4 ⇒v1v2=2:1

questions.q: Electron beam used in an electron microscope, when accelerated by a voltage of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>20</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kV</mi></math> has a de-Broglie wavelength of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><msub><mi>λ</mi><mn>0</mn></msub></math>. If the voltage is increased to <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>40</mn><mo> </mo><mi>kV</mi></math> then the de-Broglie wavelength associated with the electron beam would be:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
The de-Broglie wavelength of an electron accelerated through potential V is 

λ=hmv=h2 m(KE)=h2 meV

where, h is Planck's constant, e is charge of electron and m is mass of electron.

From above relation, λ∝1V

∴ λλ0=2040

⇒ λ=λ02.

questions.q: In a photoelectric effect experiment, the graph of stopping potential V versus reciprocal of wavelength obtained is shown in the figure. As the intensity of incident radiation is increased :
options: Slope of the straight line get more steep
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Einstein's photoelectric equation is given by,

eVs=hν-Wo, where Wo is the work function.

⇒Vs=hceλ-Woe, where c=νλ.

Intensity does not affect the frequency and work function of a material. Therefore, the graph does not change with increasing intensity.

questions.q: Consider an electron in a hydrogen atom, revolving in its second excited state (having radius <math><mn>4.65</mn><mi> </mi><mtext>Å</mtext></math> ). The de-Broglie wavelength of this electron is:
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
According to Bohr’s atomic model
mvr=nh2π
And the de-Broglie wavelength
λ=hmv
From the above two equations we can write, λ=2πrn
In the 2nd excited state
λ=2πr3
∴  λ=23π×4.65  Å=9.7 Å

questions.q: Two sources of light emit with a power of <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>200</mn><mo> </mo><mi mathvariant="normal">W</mi></math>. The ratio of number of photons of visible light emitted by each source having wavelengths <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>300</mn><mo> </mo><mi>nm</mi></math> and <math xmlns="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML"><mn>500</mn><mo> </mo><mi>nm</mi></math> respectively, will be :
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Let n1 and n2 be the number of photons coming out from the first and the second source of light respectively per second.

So, for the first source,

n1×hcλ1=200   ...1

And, for the second source,

n2×hcλ2=200   ...2

From equations (1) and (2), it implies that

n1n2=λ1λ2=300500⇒n1n2=35

Order of mass me<mp<mn<mα

questions.q: A small mirror of mass $m$ is suspended by a massless thread of length $l$. Then the small angle through which the thread will be deflected when a short pulse of laser of energy $E$ falls normal on the mirror ( $\mathrm{c}=$ speed of light in vacuum and $\mathrm{g}=$ acceleration due to gravity)
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Force due to beam assuming complete reflection $\mathrm{F}=\frac{2 \mathrm{P}}{\mathrm{C}}=\frac{2}{\mathrm{C}} \frac{\mathrm{dE}}{\mathrm{dt}} ; \mathrm{P}$ is power
So change in momentum of mirror.
$\mathrm{m}(\mathrm{~V}-0)=\int \mathrm{Fdt}=\frac{2}{\mathrm{C}} \int \mathrm{dE}=\frac{2 \mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{C}}$
Now using work energy theorem ...(1)
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{W}_{\mathrm{g}}=\Delta \mathrm{k} \\ & -\mathrm{mg} \ell(1-\cos \theta)=0-\frac{1}{2} \mathrm{mv}^2 \\ & \mathrm{~g} \ell\left(2 \sin ^2 \frac{\theta}{2}\right)=\frac{\mathrm{v}^2}{2}
\end{aligned}$
as $\theta$ is small
$\begin{aligned} & \mathrm{g} \ell 2\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)^2=\frac{1}{2} \frac{4 \mathrm{E}^2}{\mathrm{~m}^2 \mathrm{c}^2} \\ & \mathrm{~g} \ell \theta^2=\frac{4 \mathrm{E}^2}{\mathrm{~m}^2 \mathrm{c}^2} \\ & \theta=\frac{2 \mathrm{E}}{\mathrm{mc} \sqrt{\mathrm{g} \ell}}\end{aligned}$

questions.q: A light source of wavelength $\lambda$ illuminates a metal surface and electrons are ejected with maximum kinetic energy of 2 eV . If the same surface is illuminated by a light source of wavelength $\frac{\lambda}{2}$, then the maximum kinetic energy of ejected electrons will be (The work function of metal is 1 eV )
questions.subject: Physics
questions.solution:
Einstein's photoelectric equation
$\begin{aligned}
& \mathrm{KE}=\frac{h c}{\lambda}=\phi_0 \\
& 2 \mathrm{eV}=\frac{h c}{\lambda}-1 \mathrm{eV} \\
& \frac{h c}{\lambda}=3 \mathrm{eV} \\
& \mathrm{KE}^{\prime}=\frac{h c}{(\lambda / 2)}-\phi_0=6 \mathrm{eV}-1 \mathrm{eV}
\end{aligned}=5 \mathrm{eV}$

λ=heEt

questions.solution:
We know that, KEmax=hf-ϕ=hcλ-ϕ

Or, hcλ-ϕ=eV0, where, ϕ=hνth and V0 is stopping potential.

So, threshold frequency is 

νth=cλ-eV0h

=3×10866330×10-10-1.6×10-19×0.426.63×10-34

=36.630×1015-1.6×0.426.63×1015

=101536.630-1.6×0.426.63=0.4524-0.1013

νth=35.11×1013
